title: Moral certainty from signs — letter example
source_text: VIII. Praeterea intellectus quandoque rei cuipiam firmum assensum praebet, non propter aliquam demonstrationem, cujus vi clare percipiat simpliciter impossibile esse ut res aliter se habeat, sed quia ex multis signis & indiciis colligit & judicat revera rem ita se habere, neque ut res sunt, & moraliter loquendo, fieri posse ut alio modo se habeat, quamvis contrarium non sit absolute impossibile. Sic vir, qui ab uxore aut viro familiari epistolam aliquam accipit non dubitat quin sit illius, sed istud pro certo sibi persuadet, eo adductus characterum ductibus, stili ratione, materia contenti, aliisque similibus: quamvis fieri possit ut malus aliquis genius simile quiddam effinxerit.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover the intellect sometimes affords firm assent to some thing not because of any demonstration by whose force it clearly perceives that it is simply impossible the thing be otherwise, but because from many signs and indications it gathers and judges that the thing truly so stands — and that, as things are and morally speaking, it cannot be that it stand another way, although the contrary is not absolutely impossible. So a man who receives some letter from his wife or a familiar friend does not doubt that it is his, but persuades himself of that as certain, led by the strokes of the characters, the manner of the style, the matter of the contents, and other like things: although it could be that some evil genius fabricated something similar.
pass_b_english: Firm assent without demonstration of absolute impossibility.
From many signs/indices: morally can’t be otherwise (contrary not absolutely impossible).
Letter example: hand, style, contents — still possible an evil genius forged it.

choices.term: quamvis contrarium non sit absolute impossibile
choices.english: although the contrary is not absolutely impossible
choices.why: Marks moral vs absolute impossibility — sets up IX’s fama species.
